summary: The machine has everything required to start building the Node.js + Mongoose multi-currency ledger against the existing Azure DocumentDB cluster: Node (npx), the documentdb MCP server (data‑plane) and Microsoft Learn search are present, Azure CLI is signed in, and a rich set of DocumentDB agent skills are installed. Several cold-answer facts were outdated or mixed up with Cosmos DB (RU) or older naming; the builder must follow the DocumentDB docs/skills (resource type = Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters, az documentdb CLI group, SRV-style connection strings with TLS and retryWrites=false, vCore/compute-tier billing model, OIDC/AAD options for data-plane, integrated search and vector features, local gateway image/port). A small set of CLI tools are missing (mongosh, azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet) but only mongosh materially helps day‑to‑day verification; the missing CLIs have workable alternatives (documentdb MCP, portal, az CLI).
summary_points: Build can start: Node (v24), npx, az (signed-in), docker and the documentdb MCP server are available and suffice to create collections, indexes, load seed data and verify queries against the live cluster.

Several cold answers were wrong/outdated: resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts), CLI group is az documentdb mongocluster (not az cosmosdb), and pricing is vCore/compute-tier + storage (not RU/s).

Connection strings use mongodb+srv with TLS and authMechanism SCRAM-SHA-256 or MONGODB-OIDC for Entra ID; the docs recommend retryWrites=false — do not rely on older cosmos-style 10255/10260 assumptions.
Local gateway image and port differ from the Cosmos emulator; the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image exposes Mongo on port 10260 for local dev (if you choose to run a local container).
Missing tools: mongosh is not on PATH (worth adding); azd/bicep/terraform/dotnet are absent but not required for this Node sample (workarounds available).
Action for builder: apply the documented corrections in the 'Guidance For Builder' section before coding (resource names/CLI commands/connection options/ idempotency index + transaction pattern).

tools.name: documentdb (MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Inspect collections, create indexes, run aggregation pipelines, sample documents, explain plans and verify what the app creates on the live cluster.
tools.detail: 18 tools exposed (list_databases, aggregate, create_index, explain, etc.)
tools.impact_if_missing: Could not verify collections/indexes or run sample queries against the live cluster; strong blocker for a sample that must verify against the live cluster.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure Portal connection strings and the portal's Query Playground or run mongosh from another host if available.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Search and fetch official Microsoft/Azure documentation to ground cold answers and confirm recommended patterns.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to verify up-to-date product facts and quickstarts; risk of using outdated patterns.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure docs via the portal or pinned internal documentation; rely on installed domain-specific skills as second-best sources.

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Read cluster metadata, firewall rules, and connection strings; optionally run az documentdb commands and verify provider registration.
tools.detail: azure-cli 2.89.1, signed in to a subscription
tools.impact_if_missing: Couldn't inspect resource state or run az documentdb mongocluster commands; verification and some setup steps would be manual in portal.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure Portal or the documentdb MCP server to inspect the cluster; ask user to provide connection strings and network configuration.

references.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

tools.name: node / npx
tools.needed_for: Build the Node.js sample, run npm install, start the Express server and run local scripts; use npx to install skill packages if needed.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run or test the Node.js sample locally.
tools.workaround: Use a different machine with node installed; use Docker to run a Node container.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optional: run the local DocumentDB Gateway image for local development and integration tests (image uses Mongo protocol on port 10260).
tools.impact_if_missing: You must test against the live cluster rather than a local Gateway container.
tools.workaround: Run tests directly against the live cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) as allowed by run policy; use the documentdb MCP server to verify DB state.

references.title: Local Deployment & Developer Workflow — Azure DocumentDB

tools.name: documentdb-azure-deployment (skill)
tools.needed_for: Authoritative guidance for resource types, CLI commands (az documentdb), Bicep/Terraform snippets, connection-string formatting and retrieval, and recommended defaults (tiers, HA).
tools.detail: Skill installed and loaded during readiness checks
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder would lack structured deployment and resource-type guidance; higher risk of using wrong CLI group/resource type.
tools.workaround: Rely on Learn documentation and the documentdb MCP server; use the Quickstart pages in Learn.

tools.name: documentdb-driver (skill)
tools.needed_for: Driver and Mongoose best practices (singleton client, connection reuse), and guidance about starting sessions for transactions.
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of writing non-production connection code (creating clients per-request) and introducing connection churn or pool exhaustion.
tools.workaround: Follow general MongoDB driver best practices and the documentdb-connection skill; include singleton pattern manually.

tools.name: documentdb-connection (skill)
tools.needed_for: Fine-tune Mongoose / mongodb driver connection options (tls, retryWrites, pool sizes) appropriate for serverless vs long-running servers.
tools.detail: Skill installed; contains specific patterns and recommended settings for Node/Azure Functions/OLTP
tools.impact_if_missing: Might pick suboptimal connection settings or set unsupported driver flags (causing connection errors).
tools.workaround: Use Learn quickstarts and the documentdb quickstart Node examples; test connections before load tests.

references.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js

tools.name: documentdb-indexing (skill)
tools.needed_for: Designing and creating indexes: unique index for idempotencyKey, indexes to support exchange-rate lookups and aggregation performance.
tools.detail: Skill installed; contains index selection & shape guidance
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of missing required unique index for idempotency or choosing inefficient index shapes.
tools.workaround: Create indexes following the Learn quickstarts and validate performance using documentdb MCP explain tool.

tools.name: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)
tools.needed_for: If the builder wants to run a local DocumentDB Gateway for dev/testing (Docker image, port 10260), this skill guides that setup.
tools.detail: Skill installed; documents Gateway image and port 10260
tools.impact_if_missing: Local gateway setup guidance would be missing; builder might attempt to use the Cosmos emulator (wrong) or fail to bind ports correctly.
tools.workaround: Use the live cluster specified by DOCUMENTDB_URI; or consult public docs for the container image.

tools.name: az login (Azure sign-in credential)
tools.needed_for: Reading resource metadata, connection strings and firewall rules via az; the inventory shows az is signed in and a subscription is active.
tools.detail: Signed-in subscription 'Visual Studio Enterprise Subscription' available
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run az commands that require subscription context; trouble verifying cluster metadata.
tools.workaround: Use the portal or ask the user to provide the connection string and firewall settings.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Manual verification, ad-hoc query exploration and index checks from a shell. Helpful but not strictly required when MCP server and portal are present.
tools.impact_if_missing: Loss of convenient local mongo shell for quick checks; manual verification must use documentdb MCP tools or portal.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server's aggregation/find tools or the Azure portal's connection playground; install mongosh or use npx mongosh to run it locally.

references.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (i.e. a Cosmos DB account).
confusions.grounded_answer: The managed Azure DocumentDB cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historical overlap: older Cosmos DB accounts used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for Cosmos DB resource types; vCore-based DocumentDB exposes a new resource type mongoClusters. Same provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and similar historical naming caused the mix-up.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses databaseAccounts and az cosmosdb commands, infra scripts will target the wrong resource type and CLI commands will fail; deployment templates and provider checks will be incorrect.
improvements: Add a clear top‑line sentence on the Azure DocumentDB quickstart and resource reference pages: 'Azure DocumentDB clusters deploy as Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (vCore offering), not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.'
On pages that still document databaseAccounts in the MongoDB context, add a deprecation/redirect note pointing to the mongoClusters docs.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example create command: az cosmosdb create ... (No extra extension required.)
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct CLI group for the vCore-managed Azure DocumentDB cluster is az documentdb mongocluster (az documentdb extension commands). The documentdb extension may prompt to install on first use; the quickstarts recommend az documentdb mongocluster create and related commands.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts / az cosmosdb) historically managed Mongo-compatible accounts; the new vCore offering uses a new az documentdb command group (documentdb extension).

confusion_sources.title: Azure CLI reference for Cosmos DB (legacy)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder runs az cosmosdb create, they will create or target the wrong (Cosmos DB) resource or get different semantics; CLI failures or the wrong billing model may result.
improvements: State clearly on the az cli quickstarts that vCore clusters use az documentdb mongocluster commands and show the az extension add --name documentdb example.
Add a short 'Which CLI should I use?' FAQ in the top-level DocumentDB quickstart distinguishing az documentdb (mongocluster) vs az cosmosdb.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account (Cosmos DB).
confusions.grounded_answer: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters in Bicep/ARM; Terraform/AzAPI and AzureRM have corresponding mongoCluster resources (azurerm_mongo_cluster / azapi resources that target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historical reuse of the Microsoft.DocumentDB namespace for Cosmos DB databaseAccounts and a previous vCore naming (Cosmos DB for MongoDB vCore) produced overlap in docs; the new dedicated mongoClusters resource should be used for Azure DocumentDB.
confusions.build_risk: IaC templates will deploy the wrong resource type; automated scripts will fail or provision Cosmos DB (RU) accounts which use a different billing model and API constraints.
improvements: Update Bicep/Terraform quickstarts to show the exact mongoClusters resource with example snippets and a note pointing out the difference to databaseAccounts.
Add a one-line mapping table 'When to use mongoClusters vs databaseAccounts' at the top of the deployment docs.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical form: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false... SRV form may be offered. Port 10255 and replicaSet=globaldb recommended.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB connection strings are mongodb+srv style to the *.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com or global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com host. Use TLS (tls=true / ssl=true), authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 for native auth or MONGODB-OIDC for Microsoft Entra ID, and the docs recommend retryWrites=false. Direct port-based hostnames are not the recommended pattern for managed DocumentDB clusters.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer reflects older Cosmos DB for MongoDB connection patterns (.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and default ports like 10255/10260) while Azure DocumentDB vCore uses mongocluster hostnames and SRV URIs; overlapping host tokens (cosmos.azure.com) and similar driver options cause confusion.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB (Mongo) historic connection string docs

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host/port or wrong driver options (e.g., leaving retryWrites=true when the service requires it false, or using replicaSet=globaldb when SRV handles routing) can cause connection failures or incorrect routing.
improvements: Add an explicit 'example connection strings' section to the quickstart with both native-SCRAM and Entra/OIDC SRV examples and call out retryWrites=false.
Add a short 'don't use port-10255 style URIs for mongoClusters' note on the connection-guides that still show older Cosmos URIs.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is billed in Cosmos DB terms using Request Units (RU/s).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore offering) is billed by compute (cluster tier in vCores/memory) and storage; there are no RU/s charges. You pick a compute tier (M10, M20, M30, M40, ...) and storage per shard. This differs from Cosmos DB (RU model).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model conflated Cosmos DB's RU-based billing (for Cosmos DB for MongoDB API) with the vCore-based Azure DocumentDB product; same provider namespace and overlapping naming caused the mix.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder expects RU/s they may design an unnecessary autoscale or RM-based billing check and misconfigure templates or cost estimates.
improvements: Clarify pricing differences prominently on the product landing page: 'DocumentDB (vCore) uses compute tiers + storage; Cosmos DB (RU-mode) uses RU/s'.
Add an explicit 'How billing differs from Cosmos DB' note on migration and quickstart pages.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary auth for the MongoDB API is username/password. Azure AD is for management plane; driver-level AAD data-plane auth is not the default path.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both native (SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) for data-plane access. The cluster can be configured to allow NativeAuth, MicrosoftEntraID, or both; Entra ID/OIDC is used via special SRV/URI patterns (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC / MONGODB-OIDC or MONGODB-OIDC parameters and authMechanismProperties) and managed identities can be registered as database principals. Entra ID for data-plane is supported and documented.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos/Mongo guidance emphasized username/password; the vCore DocumentDB product added OIDC/AAD support and the docs and CLIs now expose auth-allowed-modes, causing older mental models to be inaccurate.

confusion_sources.title: Legacy guidance that treats AAD as management-plane only

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes AAD isn't available for data-plane, they may implement insecure password handling or miss the opportunity to use managed identities and token-based auth.
improvements: Add a short 'Entra ID for data-plane is supported' FAQ on the connection docs and show a concrete OIDC SRV example and managed-identity steps for apps running in Azure.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB API use standard MongoDB drivers (mongodb npm driver and Mongoose). No separate SDK.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (the official mongodb driver) and Mongoose on top of it for ODM patterns. There's no special proprietary DocumentDB SDK for data-plane MongoDB usage; management tasks use az / ARM / Bicep.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none
confusions.build_risk: none

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Newer vector-capable offerings reference algorithms such as HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. Example db.collection.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { vectorOptions: { algorithm: 'hnsw', dims: 1536 } }).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports integrated vector index types (cosmosSearch subtypes): DiskANN, HNSW and IVF. The service exposes creation/query via the DocumentDB-specific createSearchIndexes/cosmosSearch APIs and index definitions — the index subsystem is documented in the vector-search guidance and the skill's vector docs (not the community createIndex format).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a generic Mongo-style createIndex shape; DocumentDB exposes vector indexes in a DocumentDB-specific index creation flow (`createSearchIndexes` + `cosmosSearch`/vector subtypes). Similar algorithm names (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) exist across vendors which led to a superficially-correct but syntactically-wrong example.

confusion_sources.title: Example community index forms for other vector DBs

confusions.build_risk: If the builder emits the wrong createIndex shape, index creation will fail; the sample must use the DocumentDB index creation commands or the documentdb MCP server to create vector indexes.
improvements: Add one small sample snippet showing how to create a DiskANN/HNSW/IVF index via createSearchIndexes in the main vector-search quickstart page (show the minimal JSON).
Add a 'vector indexing' example to the Node quickstart demonstrating index creation via the management API or via the documentdb MCP server.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) for full-text and hybrid search integrated with Cosmos DB; the MongoDB API doesn't expose a full-text engine.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB includes an integrated full-text search engine (createSearchIndexes + $search) and supports hybrid (BM25 + vector) retrieval using the native search + cosmosSearch primitives — you do not need a separate Azure Cognitive Search instance for integrated FTS / hybrid search in DocumentDB.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many Cosmos DB workflows recommend Azure Cognitive Search for SQL/Core APIs; that pattern propagated to Mongo examples. DocumentDB exposes an integrated search index and $search stage which differs from a separate Azure Cognitive Search integration.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cognitive Search + Cosmos DB integration pages (for other APIs)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder tries to pipe data into Azure Cognitive Search unnecessarily they will build extra infra and add complexity; instead use createSearchIndexes and $search inside the aggregation pipeline.
improvements: Make the integrated DocumentDB $search story prominent on the search guidance and on the product landing page so builders don't default to Azure Cognitive Search for DocumentDB-managed workloads.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API implements a range of versions historically up to 6.x/7.x; expect unsupported server-side JavaScript, some aggregation stages, and admin commands.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB publishes supported server-wire versions (5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 8.0 on modern clusters) and documents high feature coverage (99.03% operator coverage). Most standard drivers and aggregation stages work but specific differences exist — test critical features. The product docs list exact supported features and incompatibilities.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged inaccuracy and mixed generalities from Cosmos/Mongo history; DocumentDB's docs publish explicit supported server versions and compatibility lists — the cold answer lacked the definitive statement.
confusions.build_risk: Using an unsupported aggregation stage or driver-server mismatch could cause runtime errors; the builder must confirm the cluster's serverVersion and pick a driver version accordingly.
improvements: Add an explicit 'driver compatibility table' to the quickstart linking common Mongoose/mongodb driver versions to supported server protocol versions for DocumentDB.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator (mcr.microsoft.com/cosmosdb/linux/azure-cosmos-emulator) on 8081; or run a MongoDB Docker image on 27017 and test app logic against it.
confusions.grounded_answer: For local Azure DocumentDB development use the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) which exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260. The Cosmos DB emulator is not the right choice for DocumentDB vCore semantics. You can still run upstream mongo:6 for app-level logic but use the DocumentDB Gateway for parity testing.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer referenced the Cosmos DB emulator and default Mongo ports, which applies to other workflows; DocumentDB supplies a Gateway image and a different recommended port (10260).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes the Cosmos emulator, local tests won't reproduce DocumentDB semantics (indexes, search, vector or auth) and may produce integration surprises when running against the live cluster.
improvements: Add a one‑line 'Local dev image and port' callout in the main quickstart to prevent developers from picking the Cosmos emulator by mistake.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams (watch()) are supported on accounts that expose the corresponding MongoDB server version; no separate portal toggle usually required.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported. For single-shard clusters they generally work by default; for multishard clusters there is a documented feature toggle (preview) and guidance to enable the 'Change streams for multishard clusters' feature in Settings. The docs also show examples and resumability semantics.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer omitted the multishard toggle nuance and the exact enabling steps for multishard environments.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder expects change streams to work unchanged on multishard clusters they may see missing events; must verify cluster settings and enable the documented feature when needed.
improvements: Document the multishard change-streams enabling steps in the quickstart change-streams page, and add a short 'enable this for multishard clusters' box.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: The service-specific MCP server is the documentdb MCP server; the general azure MCP server does not substitute for the documentdb-specific tools.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. The documentdb MCP server provides data-plane tools (find, aggregate, explain, createIndex) for the service; the azure MCP server is complementary and for control-plane operations.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none
confusions.build_risk: none

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally launched a service called DocumentDB which later evolved and was rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB. Cosmos DB is not the same as any separate open-source 'DocumentDB' project.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly true but incomplete and potentially misleading: the product named 'Azure DocumentDB' today is the vCore-based offering that was previously referred to as 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)'—Microsoft clarified that Azure DocumentDB is a distinct vCore-managed service built on the open-source DocumentDB engine. It is not the same as Amazon DocumentDB or the older 'DocumentDB' name used for Cosmos DB historically. The relationship to Cosmos DB is: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is a separate offering from Cosmos DB (RU/s) though they share naming history and the same provider namespace.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Name re-use and rebranding over time (the old Azure DocumentDB → Cosmos DB rename, and later reintroduction of the 'Azure DocumentDB' name for the vCore product) caused historical names to overlap.
confusions.build_risk: Documentation or README that uses the older name may mislead users about billing model and features; clear naming must be used in the sample docs to avoid confusion.
improvements: Add a short 'Naming and relationship' paragraph on the product landing and quickstart pages summarizing: 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore) — product X; Cosmos DB (RU) — product Y; Amazon DocumentDB — unrelated service.'

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB uses Microsoft’s proprietary engine and a MongoDB wire-protocol translator; not running upstream mongod.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the product's engine), not upstream mongod; however it implements the MongoDB wire protocol for compatibility. Most application code using standard MongoDB drivers works, but there are documented behavioral differences and operator mismatches to verify.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer conflated Cosmos DB's Mongo wire proxy model with the DocumentDB engine story; the current vCore DocumentDB product explicitly cites use of the open-source DocumentDB engine.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB architecture and wire-proxy explanations

confusions.build_risk: If builders assume a MongoDB server binary underneath, they may expect identical admin commands or behavior; tests must be run and compatibility checked. Use the compatibility reference.
improvements: Add one short line in the quickstart: 'DocumentDB uses the open-source DocumentDB engine and implements MongoDB compatibility—verify the compatibility matrix before using advanced server features.'

confusions.question: What exact connection URI will the sample read at runtime and where is it stored?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the MongoDB-style URI from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI; example pattern mongodb://... or mongodb+srv://... with retryWrites=false.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the sample should read the SRV-style connection URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime. The cluster connection-string should be treated as a secret and not committed to repo artifacts. The docs recommend SRV form (mongodb+srv) with tls=true, authMechanism SCRAM-SHA-256 or MONGODB-OIDC and retryWrites=false where applicable.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none
confusions.build_risk: None if you read from DOCUMENTDB_URI and keep it out of repo.

confusions.question: Which database name and collections will the sample use and create?
confusions.cold_answer: Use database sample_fintech_07. Collections: transactions, exchange_rates, idempotency (or unique index on transactions.idempotency_key).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct for this sample: use the provided database name sample_fintech_07 and create transactions and exchange_rates collections. Enforce idempotency by a unique index on transactions.idempotencyKey (or a dedicated idempotency collection plus unique index).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none
confusions.build_risk: If the unique index is not created, idempotency can't be reliably enforced at the DB level.

confusions.question: What exact Mongoose connection options should be used to connect to Cosmos's Mongo API right now?
confusions.cold_answer: mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, ssl: true, replicaSet: 'globaldb', retryWrites: false, serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 30000 });
confusions.grounded_answer: Use mongoose.connect(DOCUMENTDB_URI) with TLS enabled in the URI (tls=true/ssl=true) and set retryWrites=false. Modern Mongoose no longer needs useNewUrlParser/useUnifiedTopology flags (they are defaults in recent versions). Do NOT assume replicaSet=globaldb; prefer SRV URIs returned by the portal. Tune pool settings via documentdb-connection skill (singleton client, pool sizes).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer included older Mongoose connection option flags and a replicaSet hint (globaldb) that are artifacts of previous Cosmos/Mongo patterns; modern Mongoose and SRV URIs make some flags unnecessary and the recommended retryWrites=false is the important service-specific flag.
confusions.build_risk: Using deprecated options or incorrect replicaSet settings could produce warnings or connection failures. Use SRV URIs from the portal and set retryWrites=false.
improvements: Update the Mongoose quickstart with a one-liner using current Mongoose versions (v9+) and an SRV connection example including tls=true and retryWrites=false.

confusions.question: How will the sample implement idempotency and what index is required?
confusions.cold_answer: Store an idempotencyKey on each transaction and enforce uniqueness via a unique index with a partialFilterExpression to only index when the key exists.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: create a unique index on transactions.idempotencyKey (unique with partialFilterExpression to allow missing keys). On incoming POST, attempt insert inside the transaction or catch duplicate-key errors (E11000) to return 409 or treat as duplicate; database-level uniqueness is the recommended enforcement.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none
confusions.build_risk: If unique index is omitted, idempotency enforcement will be unreliable under concurrency.

confusions.question: How will the sample perform multi-document transactions with Mongoose against the cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Use MongoDB transactions via sessions: startSession(), withTransaction(), pass { session } to each operation; use readConcern 'snapshot' and writeConcern majority. Ensure the account compatibility supports transactions.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct in approach. Use mongoose.startSession() and session.withTransaction(async () => { ops with { session } }) and ensure the cluster/serverVersion supports transactions. DocumentDB supports multi-document transactions; the sample should set session options and pass the session to all operations inside the transaction.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none
confusions.build_risk: If the cluster does not support transactions for the selected serverVersion or mis-specified session usage (e.g., not passing session to each write), atomicity will be broken.

information_gaps.title: Pinned Mongoose / mongodb driver compatibility matrix
information_gaps.description: No single Learn page or skill gives a concise, one-row mapping from Node (Mongoose) versions to the exact supported MongoDB wire-protocol versions for Azure DocumentDB clusters. The builder must pick a driver version compatible with the cluster's serverVersion and test it. I looked in Learn quickstarts, documentdb-driver and documentdb-azure-deployment but found no single mapping table for Mongoose->mongodb-driver->serverVersion.

information_gaps.title: Seed data canonical sample
information_gaps.description: The prompt expects a seed script but no skill/doc provides the exact sample payload, natural keys and the recommended idempotent upsert strategy for exchange_rates and transactions. I searched the prompt review, documentdb-local-deployment and quickstarts but did not find a ready-made seed dataset for the ledger scenario.

information_gaps.title: Exact transaction lifetime / timeout for sessions
information_gaps.description: The documentation notes a 30‑second maximum transaction lifetime in some examples, but there isn't a single authoritative page enumerating the supported max transaction duration and recommended retry behaviour for long-running aggregation/update combinations. I checked the Mongoose quickstart and change-stream docs but did not find a short definitive parameter table describing transaction lifetime limits.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource (and az documentdb mongocluster CLI) — do not target Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts or az cosmosdb for the vCore Azure DocumentDB cluster.

Use SRV-style connection URIs from the portal (mongodb+srv://<user>@<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/...), ensure tls=true, set retryWrites=false, and prefer authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 for native auth or MONGODB-OIDC for Microsoft Entra ID when using token/managed-identity authentication.

If you want local parity, run the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (DocumentDB local) and connect to port 10260 for Mongo protocol tests; do not rely on the Cosmos DB emulator for DocumentDB vCore semantics.

inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample because the run environment already has a cluster. If you want Terraform-based IaC verification, install Terraform per HashiCorp docs.
